newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS opens Nazi gold archives to auditors.
newsitem.headline: BIS opens Nazi gold archives to auditors.

text.p: The Bank for International Settlements (BIS) has invited a leading auditing firm to review its archives to show it has nothing to hide over its dealings in Nazi gold during World War Two, authoritative sources said on Wednesday.

The firm is believed to be one of three hired by an independent panel headed by former U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Paul Volcker to probe allegations that Swiss banks are sitting on unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims.
The auditors arrived at Basle-based BIS, which acts as central bank to the worlds' central banks, this week and are expected to conclude their review in about a month.
"We are doing this so there is full understanding of the operations undertaken by BIS during the war," one source said.

BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution, has always stressed its willingness to open its books to any authorities that wished to examine its records, including the Volcker commission or the Berne-appointed commission that is looking into Switzerland's dealings with Nazi Germany.
Two years ago BIS hired a historian to look at its archives and prepare them for historical research and the eventual opening of its files, the sources said.
The historian has prepared a detailed account of the organisation's dealings with Nazi Germany.
This report, which already has been sent to U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato, will form the basis for the auditor's work.

BIS has been drawn into the current debate over the fate of Jewish accounts in Swiss banks because of its dealings with the Reichsbank, Germany's central bank prior to the defeat of Nazi Germany in 1945.
BIS, however, is owned by central banks and only provides services to them. Private people cannot conduct banking business with it.
D'Amato, who is spearheading U.S. inquiries into dormant Jewish accounts in Switzerland, wrote to BIS general manager Andrew Crockett last year, asking him to open its records covering Nazi gold.
BIS' responded that it would fully cooperate with D'Amato's inquiry and sent him the historian's 20 page document, outlining its dealings with Germany.
BIS was founded in 1930 to help oversee reparations from Germany to the Allied governments after World War One.

The Reichsbank deposited 12 tonnes of gold in its account with the BIS between 1939 and 1945. About half of the gold was interest paid by the Reichsbank for BIS investments in Germany under the 1930 Hague Agreement and Young Plan that established the BIS as an institution.
The remainder covered German debts in a European postal clearing system and payments to Yugoslav railways.
Following World War Two and the Paris Reparation Agreement of 1946, BIS handed back to the Allied Powers 3.7 tonnes of gold.
The gold was identified as having been looted by the Nazis from occupied countries and deposited by the Reichsbank at BIS.
